stem: In 2 Samuel 12, how does the prophet Nathan bring King David to see his own wrong?
options: he reads him the lost book of the law from the temple
he tells of a rich man who took a poor man's lamb
he tears a new cloak into twelve pieces before him
he writes the king's sin upon the palace wall
why: Nathan tells David of a rich man who took a poor man's one ewe lamb; when David burns with anger, Nathan says, "Thou art the man." 2 Samuel 12:1–7.

es.stem: En 2 Samuel 12, ¿cómo hace el profeta Natán que el rey David vea su propia falta?
options: le lee el libro perdido de la ley hallado en el templo
le cuenta de un rico que le quitó al pobre su oveja
rompe un manto nuevo en doce pedazos frente a él
escribe el pecado del rey en el muro del palacio
es.why: Natán le cuenta a David de un rico que le quitó al pobre su única corderita; cuando David se enciende de ira, Natán le dice: "Tú eres ese hombre". 2 Samuel 12:1–7.

stem: In his letter to the Romans, written on his way to martyrdom, what does Ignatius of Antioch call himself?
options: a voice crying out in the wilderness of Rome
a lamp lit for Rome, set high upon its stand
a servant of the servants of God in Rome
God's wheat, ground by the teeth of beasts
why: Ignatius writes: "I am the wheat of God, and am ground by the teeth of the wild beasts, that I may be found the pure bread of Christ." Ignatius, Letter to the Romans 4.
source: Ignatius of Antioch, Letter to the Romans 4

es.stem: En su carta a los romanos, escrita camino al martirio, ¿cómo se llama a sí mismo Ignacio de Antioquía?
options: una voz que clama en el desierto de Roma
una lámpara encendida en lo alto para Roma
un siervo de los siervos de Dios en Roma
trigo de Dios, molido por dientes de fieras
es.why: Ignacio escribe: "Soy trigo de Dios, y soy molido por los dientes de las fieras para ser hallado pan puro de Cristo". Ignacio, Carta a los romanos 4.

stem: At the council in Jerusalem described in Acts 15, what did the apostles and elders decide about Gentile believers?
options: they need not be circumcised to join the church
they must be circumcised before they are baptized
they must keep every food law found in Leviticus
they should gather apart from the Jewish believers
why: After Peter and James speak, the council decides not to "trouble" Gentiles who turn to God with circumcision and the whole law, asking only a few abstentions; a letter carries the decision to Antioch. Acts 15:1–29.

es.stem: En el concilio de Jerusalén que narra Hechos 15, ¿qué decidieron los apóstoles y ancianos sobre los creyentes gentiles?
options: no necesitan circuncidarse para pertenecer
deben circuncidarse antes de ser bautizados
deben guardar cada ley de comida del Levítico
deben reunirse aparte de los creyentes judíos
es.why: Después de que hablan Pedro y Santiago, el concilio decide no "inquietar" con la circuncisión y toda la ley a los gentiles que se vuelven a Dios, y les pide solo unas pocas abstenciones; una carta lleva la decisión a Antioquía. Hechos 15:1–29.

stem: Against the teaching of Arius, what did the Council of Nicaea (325) affirm with the Greek word homoousios?
options: the Son is of like substance to the Father
the Son was the first and highest of creatures
the Son is of one substance with the Father
the Father and Son are one person in two modes
why: Arius taught that the Son was created; Nicaea answered that the Son is homoousios, "of one substance" (one being) with the Father, "true God from true God." Nicene Creed of 325.
source: Council of Nicaea (325), the Nicene Creed

es.stem: Frente a la enseñanza de Arrio, ¿qué afirmó el Concilio de Nicea (325) con la palabra griega homoousios?
options: el Hijo es de sustancia semejante al Padre
el Hijo fue la primera y más alta criatura
el Hijo es de una sustancia con el Padre
Padre e Hijo son una persona en dos modos
es.why: Arrio enseñaba que el Hijo fue creado; Nicea respondió que el Hijo es homoousios, "de la misma sustancia" (un solo ser) que el Padre, "Dios verdadero de Dios verdadero". Credo de Nicea de 325.

stem: During the iconoclast controversy, on what main ground did John of Damascus defend the making of icons?
options: an icon holds the very soul of the saint it shows
the emperor alone may rule on how the church worships
icons are older than the written gospels themselves
God became visible in Christ, so he can be pictured
why: John of Damascus argued that the invisible God could not be pictured, but in the incarnation God became visible in the flesh, so Christ may be painted: "I do not worship matter; I worship the Creator of matter." On the Divine Images.
source: John of Damascus, On the Divine Images

es.stem: Durante la controversia iconoclasta, ¿con qué argumento principal defendió Juan Damasceno la creación de íconos?
options: un ícono contiene el alma misma del santo que muestra
solo el emperador puede decidir cómo adora la iglesia
los íconos son más antiguos que los evangelios escritos
Dios se hizo visible en Cristo, y puede ser pintado
es.why: Juan Damasceno argumentó que al Dios invisible no se le podía pintar, pero en la encarnación Dios se hizo visible en la carne, así que se puede pintar a Cristo: "No adoro la materia; adoro al Creador de la materia". Sobre las imágenes divinas.

stem: A friend says that in Christ the divine nature swallowed up the human, like a drop of vinegar lost in the sea. According to the Definition of the Council of Chalcedon (451), what is wrong with that picture?
options: he is two persons who share one will between them
his two natures remain, unconfused and unchanged
his human nature began only when he was baptized
his divine nature left him before he died on the cross
why: Chalcedon confesses one Christ "in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation," each nature keeping its own properties. The Definition of Chalcedon (451); some ancient churches did not accept this wording.
source: Council of Chalcedon (451), the Definition of Faith

es.stem: Un amigo dice que en Cristo la naturaleza divina absorbió a la humana, como una gota de vinagre perdida en el mar. Según la Definición del Concilio de Calcedonia (451), ¿qué falla en esa imagen?
options: él es dos personas que comparten una sola voluntad
sus dos naturalezas siguen, sin confusión ni cambio
su naturaleza humana empezó solo cuando fue bautizado
su naturaleza divina lo dejó antes de morir en la cruz
es.why: Calcedonia confiesa un solo Cristo "en dos naturalezas, sin confusión, sin cambio, sin división, sin separación", y cada naturaleza conserva sus propiedades. Definición de Calcedonia (451); algunas iglesias antiguas no aceptaron esta formulación.

stem: In 2 Kings 2, what does Elisha ask of Elijah before Elijah is taken up, and what first shows that Elisha has received it?
why: Elisha asks for a double portion of Elijah's spirit; Elijah says it will be his if he sees him taken. He sees Elijah go up by a whirlwind with a chariot of fire, takes up the fallen mantle, strikes the Jordan, and the waters part. 2 Kings 2:9–14.

rubric.point: Says Elisha asks for a double portion of Elijah's spirit. Asking only for 'his blessing' or 'his power' without the double portion counts as partly.
Says Elisha strikes the Jordan with Elijah's mantle (cloak) and the waters part, as Elijah had done. 'He did a miracle' with no detail counts as partly.
Mentions the condition that Elisha must see Elijah taken, or the chariot and horses of fire and the whirlwind (optional, strengthens).

es.stem: En 2 Reyes 2, ¿qué le pide Eliseo a Elías antes de que Elías sea llevado, y qué muestra primero que Eliseo lo recibió?
es.why: Eliseo pide una doble porción del espíritu de Elías; Elías le dice que la tendrá si lo ve cuando sea llevado. Lo ve subir en un torbellino con un carro de fuego, recoge el manto caído, golpea el Jordán y las aguas se abren. 2 Reyes 2:9–14.

stem: In the Martyrdom of Polycarp, what is the old bishop of Smyrna urged to do to save his life, and how does he answer?
why: The proconsul urges Polycarp to swear by Caesar's fortune and revile Christ; he answers: "Eighty and six years have I served him, and he has done me no wrong. How then can I blaspheme my King who saved me?" He is then put to death. Martyrdom of Polycarp 9–16.

rubric.point: Says he is urged to curse or revile Christ (or to swear by the emperor's fortune). 'Give up his faith' in general counts as partly.
Gives the gist of his answer: he has served Christ eighty-six years and Christ has done him no wrong, so he cannot curse his King. Refusing without the reason counts as partly.
Mentions that he is then put to death in the arena, at the stake by fire, or by a dagger when the flames did not harm him (optional, strengthens).

es.stem: En el Martirio de Policarpo, ¿qué presionan al anciano obispo de Esmirna a hacer para salvar su vida, y cómo responde?
es.why: El procónsul presiona a Policarpo para que jure por la fortuna del César e insulte a Cristo; él responde: "Ochenta y seis años lo he servido, y ningún mal me ha hecho. ¿Cómo puedo blasfemar contra mi Rey que me salvó?". Luego le dan muerte. Martirio de Policarpo 9–16.
